_comment: Editorial summaries of each hunt for the website. The README in hunts/<ID>/ is the source of truth; these numbers are copied from its funnel table. A hunt whose directory is missing is skipped, so an entry can land before its hunt merges.

hunts.title: Weighing dark lenses with Gaia
hunts.question: Only one isolated stellar-mass black hole is known. When a dark object passes in front of a star it brightens the star and also shifts its position by a fraction of a milliarcsecond, and the shift reveals the lens mass. Can Gaia DR4's first per-transit positions weigh the lenses of Oddsky's own long microlensing events?
hunts.state: engine built and refereed; forecasts sealed; runs on Gaia DR4 day
hunts.scale: 109 lens targets in DR4's span · 325 matched control stars · 2,900 simulated lenses for the acceptance test
funnel: lens targets inside Gaia DR4's span
known OGLE/KMTNet events kept as controls
hunts.verdict: A joint brightening-and-position fitter, tested on thousands of simulated lenses at the real target positions: a 10 solar-mass lens is detected 77% of the time for a bright star and 23% for a faint one, and no lighter lens was ever mistaken for a black hole. The honest chance of a black-hole claim from DR4 is about one in ten; any deflection goes to a referee first. Five forecasts are sealed.

hunts.title: Gaia DR4 day
hunts.question: Gaia DR4 (2 December 2026) publishes 5.5 years of measurements for some 2.8 billion sources, the largest time-domain release yet. What can be tested, and found, within hours of release?
hunts.state: pipeline built and rehearsed on DR3; forecasts sealed
hunts.scale: one command · 26 sealed predictions · rehearsal on DR3 found nothing new and four bugs
funnel: Gaia classifier lenses absent from DR3's catalogue, re-tested
strong NEOWISE events in DR4's span
hunts.verdict: A one-command release-day pipeline: it confirms what ESA released, grades every sealed prediction, and runs targeted searches on Oddsky's candidate lists. The DR3 rehearsal reproduced earlier results exactly and caught a format change that would have broken every DR4 light curve, fixed in advance. Five search forecasts are sealed.

hunts.title: Stars that make dust on a schedule
hunts.question: Some massive binary stars throw off a shell of dust each time their two stars swing close, so they brighten in the infrared on a fixed period. Fewer than a dozen are known outside our galaxy. What does a systematic search of fourteen years of WISE data, extended with Spitzer back to 2004, find in 318 nearby galaxies?
hunts.state: first full run done and refereed; three new repeating sources are cases
hunts.scale: 318 galaxies within 10 Mpc · 25,365 light curves · WISE 2010-2024 + Spitzer 2004-2019 · 1,433 injection tests
funnel: new repeating sources opened as cases (OS-0033, OS-0034, OS-0035)
hunts.verdict: The search recovers the NGC 2403 source (OS-0031) blind, with four cycles from 2007 to 2022. It also shows that very luminous dusty pulsating stars can mimic a dust maker in WISE data alone, so the light-curve shape and a third cycle from Spitzer decide. Two new periodic candidates survive: a source in NGC 4945 with three sharp outbursts every 5.4 years, and one in NGC 3344, next to Wolf-Rayet stars, that flares about every 10 years like the famous dust maker WR 140. A third source in M81 erupted twice, 14 years apart.

hunts.title: Vanishing and appearing stars in nearby galaxies
hunts.question: Stars that collapse into black holes without a bright supernova, and explosions hidden by dust, should still show up in the mid-infrared. What does a difference-imaging search of every star-forming galaxy within 10 Mpc in fourteen years of WISE data find?
hunts.state: v2 rerun done and refereed; three discoveries are cases
hunts.scale: 318 galaxies within 10 Mpc · 334 unWISE tiles · 25 epochs 2010-2024 · 25,454 variable sources (v2)
funnel: not ordinary pulsating or irregular variables
not foreground stars, quasars or known objects
hunts.verdict: Run blind, the new tool recovers the known failed-supernova candidates M31-2014-DS1 and N6946-BH1 and over a dozen known supernovae, red novae and dust-enshrouded transients. Its first discovery is an infrared flare in NGC 3239 in 2020 that no optical survey saw, now registered with the IAU as AT 2020afkm and described in TNS AstroNote 2026-308: Hubble caught a faint point source 85 days later that has since vanished, and JWST found cooling dust at the same spot in 2024. K. De's group, who flagged it independently in 2022, favour a very dusty nova from a near-infrared spectrum. The improved second run found a hidden infrared source in NGC 2403 that has flared every 5.3 years since 2007 (a dust-making binary or an extreme pulsating star; next outburst due around 2028.5) and a luminous star in NGC 55 whose dust is clearing. Four more infrared-only outbursts (NGC 4945, M81, NGC 55, IC 342) are being followed.

hunts.title: Gaia's unpublished lenses
hunts.question: Gaia's own variability classifier labels 254 stars as microlensing events, but 67 of them never made it into Gaia's published microlensing catalogue. Oddsky's blind NEOWISE search had already found three of them. What are the other 64?
hunts.scale: 67 Gaia DR3 sources · Gaia DR3 epoch photometry · NEOWISE · OGLE, KMTNet, Gaia alerts, TNS, SIMBAD as references
funnel: classifier MICROLENSING, not in Gaia's catalogue
Oddsky cases found blind (OS-0026, OS-0027, OS-0029)
apparently unreported lens candidates after the referee (3 strong)
hunts.verdict: The list was known (Rimoldini et al. 2023 counted the 67) but nobody had vetted it. Nine look like microlensing events nobody has reported, three of them strong, and about 5 to 10 are expected to be real. They fell where nobody was watching: outside OGLE's alert fields, or in the months when the bulge is too close to the Sun for ground telescopes while Gaia kept scanning. Gaia's catalogue also left out 28 lenses other surveys knew, including the famous binary lens Gaia16aye.

hunts.title: The long lenses
hunts.question: The lensing-sky search could not see saturated peaks, events lasting longer than one NEOWISE visit, or stars beside a bright neighbour. Black-hole lenses would hide exactly there. What does a search without those blind spots find?
hunts.state: survey done; six Gaia DR4 predictions sealed
hunts.scale: 211.7 million stars · 108.3 billion NEOWISE detections · the whole sky
funnel: single-peaked brightenings, one to six visits
clean, not at the first or last visit
strong and unexplained, not yet followed up
hunts.verdict: Searching the stars the first pass skipped, those beside bright neighbours and those blended with others, matters more than the new rule for long events. The search now finds 118 known microlensing events instead of 64, and 43 of 353 catchable ones instead of 18, with the biggest gain in the crowded bulge. Its 122 strong unexplained brightenings, many of them long and colour-neutral, are where a black-hole lens would be; Six events that no optical survey caught, or that ATLAS confirmed, now carry sealed predictions for Gaia DR4, due 2 December 2026.

hunts.title: The lensing sky
hunts.question: When a foreground star passes almost exactly in front of a background one, it acts as a lens and the background star brightens equally at every wavelength. NEOWISE looked at every star twice a year for ten years. How many lenses did it see?
hunts.state: survey done, refereed; one new event reproduced
hunts.scale: 194.7 million stars · 106.7 billion NEOWISE detections · the whole sky including the Galactic plane · KMTNet, OGLE, Gaia and ZTF as references
funnel: apparently unreported: one microlensing event (OS-0018), one candidate (OS-0019)
hunts.verdict: Without being told where to look, the search recovered 64 microlensing events that KMTNet, OGLE, Gaia and ZTF had already found, and none of the matches is a coincidence. It also found one nobody seems to have reported: OS-0018, a giant that brightened 5.4 times in September 2022 over about four months. ATLAS caught the whole event, and a point lens fits it from the optical to 4.6 microns. A second, OS-0019, brightened once by 60% but no simple lens fits it, so it stays a candidate. ATLAS follow-up of the southern events adds four more candidates, two of them unclassified Gaia alerts. NEOWISE is a real but partial lens detector: good for bright stars in the Galactic disk, nearly blind in the crowded bulge, and unable to see saturated peaks.
hunts.figure_caption: Every HEALPix pixel searched (grey, by number of stars) and every clean one-night brightening, coloured by what it turned out to be. Stars: microlensing events, known (orange) and new or unreported (red: OS-0016 to OS-0019).

hunts.title: One night in the infrared
hunts.question: NEOWISE looked at every star for about a day, twice a year, for ten years. Which ordinary stars were dramatically different on just one of those days?
hunts.scale: 79,191 NEOWISE light curves (W1 < 13, |b| ≥ 10°) · IRSA single exposures, Gaia DR3, ZTF, ATLAS, TESS
funnel: one-visit events, equal in W1 and W2
stellar colours, not at the first or last visit
hunts.verdict: The method works: blind, it found OS-0014, a dozen dwarf novae in outburst and two microlensing events Gaia had already caught. What nobody had reported: a red giant toward the Galactic anticentre that brightened sevenfold for a few weeks in 2017, seen by NEOWISE and ATLAS on the same night. It is a microlensing event. The lens mass is not measured; Gaia DR4 should settle it. A pass over 7,804 fainter stars turned up a second event: a halo giant that brightened at least 2.4 times in March 2020, seen by NEOWISE, ATLAS and ZTF.

hunts.title: The Gaia alerts nobody finished
hunts.question: Gaia flagged thousands of stars that faded, then moved on. What did the unexplained ones do before and after it looked?
hunts.scale: 27,076 Gaia alerts · Pan-STARRS, WISE, ZTF, ATLAS, TESS, CRTS, 2MASS and Palomar plates 1954-2026
funnel: not a known class or a young star
hunts.verdict: Every survivor was already a catalogued variable; what is new is what they are. One star has spent most of the last 35 years 3-5 magnitudes fainter. Another, catalogued as a nova-like, is an old dusty dwarf that keeps going dark.

hunts.title: Stars that go dark
hunts.question: Which of the 2,356 stars the experts short-listed as R Coronae Borealis candidates have gone dark since anyone last looked?
hunts.scale: 2,401 candidates · ZTF and ATLAS 2015-2026 · calibrated on 48 known R CrB and dLHdC stars
funnel: R CrB candidates from WISE colours and Gaia
a fast, unscheduled fade of ≥ 1 mag
worth a case after a human looked
hunts.verdict: No new R CrB star yet: every northern fader was already in a catalogue. The survivor is stranger: a dust-shrouded star eclipsed year after year on a 385.7-day clock, confirmed independently by ATLAS.

hunts.title: Infrared afterglows on Sun-like stars
hunts.question: Which Sun-like stars suddenly grew hot dust, the infrared glow of a planetary collision, seen from any angle?
hunts.scale: 146.6 billion NEOWISE detections · 164.7 million stars · 1 h 53 min on 24 spot VMs · a few dollars
funnel: real stars with a Gaia parallax
the glow sits on the star
hunts.verdict: ASASSN-21qj recovered blind at 46σ. One survivor vanished for 95 days in 2017. A re-run with a bug fixed tested 24.5 million photospheres instead of 18.1 million and found no new survivor.

hunts.title: Sun-like stars that Gaia caught fading
hunts.question: Which main-sequence stars did Gaia see dim between 2014 and 2017, and which has nobody explained?
hunts.scale: Gaia DR3 variability catalogue · ZTF · TESS
hunts.verdict: Two new eclipsing binaries, which Gaia's pipeline had given periods of 53 and 36 minutes instead of 2.5 and 11.9 days. And one 'invisible companion' that our own referee proved was a folding alias before anyone announced it.

hunts.title: New R CrB stars in Gaia DR3
hunts.question: Can Gaia's 2014-17 light curves turn up R Coronae Borealis stars the experts missed?
hunts.verdict: Parked. The experts had already mined Gaia DR3; our best candidates were a VY Scl binary, a Mira, an S star and a T Tauri star.

wrong.title: The invisible companion that wasn't
wrong.text: We folded a binary at a fifth of its period, and a Sun-sized dark object appeared. A referee agent told to break it found the alias in 30 minutes. Nothing was announced; the tool now checks for it.

wrong.title: A bug in our own grader
wrong.text: Trial 001's grader hid real outbursts and marked two correct forecasts false. We fixed it after the reveal, so both gradings are published.

wrong.title: Five overstatements about EE Cep
wrong.text: Our measurement of the 2025 eclipse held up. Our claim that nobody else was watching did not: professional campaigns were. The referee struck it.

wrong.title: A quarter of the testable stars, quietly skipped
wrong.text: A float conversion made neighbouring star ids equal, so each star's first NEOWISE visit was blended with its neighbour's and many steady stars looked noisy. The survivors stood; the fixed re-run searched 24.5 million stars instead of 18.1 million and found nothing new.

wrong.title: A clock that wasn't, and a Sun-like star that isn't
wrong.text: We fitted a 392-day period to four dips of an old K dwarf and predicted the next one. The referee fetched older surveys and found deep dips at the wrong phases; the sky agreed, with no dip on the predicted date. We also called a star Sun-like from a Gaia fit that had failed; it shows strong H-alpha emission.

wrong.title: A parallax we measured too precisely
wrong.text: We fitted the 2017 event and quoted the lens's parallax to ±12% and a lens mass. A second referee showed half of that parallax moves with a 1% calibration offset in one ATLAS telescope, and that other motions fit as well. The range is now 0.6-1.6, and the mass is not measured.

wrong.title: A dwarf nova we briefly thought was new
wrong.text: Our variable-star catalogue lookups started returning a CAPTCHA page after ~150 queries, and our script read it as 'no match'. For an hour DX And, a dwarf nova known for decades, looked like a discovery. Lookups now go through a mirror and report errors as errors.

wrong.title: A peak three weeks off
wrong.text: From NEOWISE and the tail in ZTF, a referee predicted when ATLAS would show this event peaking, and how bright. ATLAS put the peak three weeks earlier and higher. The model had no parallax, which bends the light curve; with it, all three surveys agree.

wrong.title: Three discoveries that weren't
wrong.text: We announced four new microlensing events in the draft. The referee found three of them in a ZTF catalogue whose full table lives only on the journal's website, and on TNS, which had been refusing our queries. One survives. We also withdrew an efficiency estimate whose model of when NEOWISE looked was off by three weeks for half the visits.

wrong.title: A cut that removed the peak
wrong.text: Our first fit of the two 2022 events threw out ATLAS frames with a poor PSF fit, but the fit gets worse as a star brightens, so the cut removed the peak. We had also compared the lens against a Gaussian, whose wings are too thin to be a fair rival. The referee caught both. OS-0018 survives every choice; OS-0019's fitted timescale did not, so it went from a fitted lens to a candidate.
